title: When Two Names Reach the Same List
content:
What problem does this solve?
Assignment does not always create a new copy. With a list, `b = a` makes both names reach the same list. If code changes that list through either name, the other name sees the change too.

Mutation versus rebinding
Appending through b changes the shared list. Writing `b = [9]` is different: b is rebound so it reaches a different list; the original list itself was not changed.

Make a separate outer list
  b = list(a)
creates a new outer list containing the same current items. Appending to b no longer appends to a. If those items are themselves mutable lists, the inner lists are still shared; one-level copying does not promise deep independence.

Functions make the contract matter
A helper may intentionally mutate its input, or it may be required to preserve the caller's list and return a separate one. Neither rule is universally correct; the function's contract must say which behavior is intended.

Vocabulary after the behavior
A reference is how a name reaches an object. Two names for the same mutable object are aliases. Mutation changes the object; rebinding changes which object a name reaches. `list(existing)` makes a shallow, one-level list copy.
concepts: Two names can refer to the same mutable list
Mutation through either alias is visible through the other
Rebinding one name does not mutate the original object
list(existing) makes a separate outer list
A shallow outer copy can still share nested mutable items
Whether a function mutates its input is part of its contract

examples.title: Two names, one list
examples.explanation: a and b reach the same list, so the append is visible through a.

examples.title: Rebinding one name
examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b = [9]
print(a)
print(b)
examples.explanation: b now reaches a new list; a still reaches the original.

examples.title: Separate outer list
examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = list(a)
b.append(3)
print(a)
print(b)
examples.explanation: The outer lists are separate, so appending to b does not alter a.

examples.title: Nested sharing remains
examples.explanation: Only the outer list was copied; both outer lists still contain the same inner list objects.

common_mistakes: Assuming b = a copies a list because there are two variable names
Using equal contents as proof that two variables are the same object
Copying only after unintended mutation already happened
Treating all mutation as bad rather than specifying the function contract
Assuming one-level copying makes arbitrary nested data fully independent

exercises.title: Two names, one list
hints: Track which list object each name reaches before the append.
b = a does not create a new list; both names reach the same one.
Appending through b makes a show [1, 2, 3].

exercises.title: Change through the other name
hints: Again, assignment made two names for one list.
Changing the list through a is visible through b.
b prints ['x', 'y'].

exercises.title: Rebinding is different
exercises.code_to_predict:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b = [9]
print(a)
print(b)
hints: The second assignment to b changes what b reaches.
No method changed the original [1, 2] list.
a prints [1, 2]; b prints [9].

exercises.title: Separate outer copy
exercises.code_to_predict:
a = [1, 2]
b = list(a)
b.append(3)
print(a)
print(b)
hints: list(a) creates another outer list.
Appending to b changes the copied list only.
a stays [1, 2]; b becomes [1, 2, 3].

exercises.title: Outer copy, inner sharing
hints: The outer list was copied, but ask what objects are stored inside both outer lists.
Both outer lists still contain the same first inner list.
Appending chalk to copied[0] changes that shared inner list, so original[0] also contains chalk.

exercises.title: Function changes its argument
exercises.code_to_predict:
def add_flag(items):
    items.append("flag")

values = ["a"]
add_flag(values)
print(values)
hints: The argument passes the list object into the parameter.
append mutates that same list rather than rebinding only the local parameter.
values therefore becomes ['a', 'flag'].

exercises.title: Preserve the caller
exercises.prompt: `add_flag` is required to leave its input list unchanged. Repair it by making a separate outer list, appending to the copy, and returning the copy.
exercises.reference_solution:
def add_flag(items):
    result = list(items)
    result.append("flag")
    return result
hints: Do not append until you have a different outer list to work with.
Create `result = list(items)`, then mutate result instead of items.
Append flag to result and return result.

exercises.title: Non-mutating helper
exercises.prompt: Write `with_item(items, item)` that returns a separate outer list containing the old values plus item. The caller's `items` list must remain unchanged.
exercises.reference_solution:
def with_item(items, item):
    result = list(items)
    result.append(item)
    return result
hints: Copy the outer list before changing anything.
Append the new item to the copied result, not to the parameter list.
Use `result = list(items)`, append item, then return result.

exercises.title: Mutation as a contract
exercises.prompt: A function named `consume_last(supplies)` is explicitly documented to remove the final supply from the caller's list. Is mutating that list acceptable?
choices: Yes, because mutation is part of the stated contract.
No, functions may never mutate arguments.
hints: Do not turn the previous exercises into a rule that mutation is always wrong.
The important question is whether the caller was promised that its list would change.
Here mutation is explicitly the contract, so it is acceptable.

exercises.title: Prepare Independent Loadouts
exercises.prompt: Write `prepare_loadouts(base, party_size)` returning a list containing `party_size` separate outer copies of `base`. Use a loop and make a new `list(base)` for each member. Mutating one returned loadout must not change `base` or any sibling loadout. `party_size = 0` should return an empty list.
hints: Start with an empty outer result list and repeat once per party member.
The copy operation must happen inside the loop so each member receives a different outer list.
Inside `for index in range(party_size)`, append `list(base)` to loadouts; return loadouts after the loop.

tests.message: Changing one returned loadout must leave its sibling and the original content unchanged.

exercises.success_message: Each party member now owns a separate outer loadout, and the base list remains untouched.
